newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hermitage treasures on show in Amsterdam.
newsitem.headline: Hermitage treasures on show in Amsterdam.

text.p: A glittering exhibition of several hundred pieces from the 18th-century collection of one of history's most acquisitive art lovers opens to the public on Tuesday.

In her three decades on the Russian throne, Austrian-born Tsarina Catherine the Great acquired more works of art than the Louvre in Paris amassed over four centuries, one of the exhibition's advisors said.
"Nothing escaped her eye -- from ornamental snuff boxes to Dutch Old Masters to entire libraries comprising several thousand books," said Maaike Nillesen.
Highpoints of the exhibition in Amsterdam's New Church include Rembrandt's Holy Family, the largest Wedgewood dinner service ever made and Catherine's highly ornate golden state coach.
"She wanted only the best -- and lots of it. She retained an army of roving ambassadors whose task it was to track down treasures and buy them for her," Nillesen added.

When Catherine died in 1796 after a 34-year reign, her collection comprised almost 4,000 paintings, tens of thousands of drawings, etchings and books, 11,000 cameos and ornamental seals and several scientific collections.
Her treasure-stuffed Winter Palace in St Petersburg, together with the annexes she decreed be built to house her burgeoning collection, are collectively better-known today as the Hermitage Museum.

But Catherine was no empty-headed shopaholic. A highly intelligent and politically astute woman, she engineered the overthrow and murder of her unpopular husband Tsar Peter III to become Russia's longest-reigning monarch.
She corresponded regularly with enlightened thinkers such as France's Voltaire, and in 1767 drew up guidelines for Russia's first formalised legal code.
However, her suggestions ran into such opposition from the Church and ruling aristocratic establishment that she was forced to abandon legal reform.
Under her reign the country underwent a cultural and political renaissance unequalled since the time of Peter The Great, the father of modern-day Russia who she deeply admired.
"St Petersburg became a centre of culture and Catherine's mania for collecting gave an enormous impetus to local industry," said Nilissen.

Entitled "Catherine, the Tsarina and the Arts", the exhibition divides roughly into two parts. The first deals with her life, her lovers -- she is said to have had more than 20 -- and her achievements, while the second focuses on the treasures of her collection.
Organised as part of the Peter The Great year marking three centuries of Russian-Dutch ties, the exhibition runs until April 13 next year.
